site.name: Romley Mining Camp & Tram Terminal
overview: Romley was a mining and railroad camp in the upper Chalk Creek district that became an important transfer point for ore from the Mary Murphy Mine. Its surviving tram terminal represents the cable-tram system that carried ore from workings high on Chrysolite Mountain to the railroad and processing facilities below.

timeline.text: Railroad development through upper Chalk Creek connected the mining camps of St. Elmo, Romley, and Hancock with outside markets and smelters.
A nearly 5,000-foot aerial tramway was built to move Mary Murphy ore down to Romley, where it could be transferred for processing and shipment.
Full-time Mary Murphy production ended in 1925, and railroad service through the area was dismantled soon afterward as mining activity declined.
The Historic American Engineering Record documented surviving Mary Murphy mining and tramway structures, including the Romley terminal.

moreHistory: Chaffee County historic-resource research identifies the Mary Murphy as the Chalk Creek district's most productive mine and describes its 4,996-foot single-cable aerial tramway. Ninety-six ore buckets, each with roughly 200-pound capacity, could move about 128 tons to the loading switch in a 24-hour period.

The Romley terminal is a rare surviving lower terminal associated with the Mary Murphy tramway. It linked mountain mining operations with the railroad transportation network that made large-scale production in the remote district practical.
